name: Samuel Austin Worcester
description: Samuel Austin Worcester was a Congregationalist missionary of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM) at New Echota in the Cherokee Nation, where he also served as federal postmaster. Convicted on September 15, 1831 under Georgia's law barring white persons from living in Cherokee territory without a state license, he and Elizur Butler alone refused the offered clemency and were imprisoned at hard labor. His appeal produced the U.S. Supreme Court's landmark decision Worcester v. Georgia (1832), holding that Georgia's laws had no force within the Cherokee Nation. He was released on January 14, 1833.

cases.charges: Residing within the Cherokee Nation without a license from the Governor and without taking the oath of allegiance to the State of Georgia, in violation of Georgia's act of December 22, 1830.
cases.sentence: Four years at hard labor. Refused the clemency terms Georgia offered the other defendants and was committed to the penitentiary at Milledgeville; released January 14, 1833 by Governor Wilson Lumpkin's discharge order following the U.S. Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia.

cases.convicted: No — released on bond to appear at the September 1831 court term.
cases.charges: Residing in the Cherokee Nation without a Georgia license (July 1831 arrest by the Georgia Guard).
cases.sentence: Arrested at New Echota, allowed to spend the first night at home because his wife was seriously ill, then marched to Camp Gilmer and taken to Lawrenceville under a writ of habeas corpus, where he posted security for the September term.

cases.convicted: No — discharged by Judge Augustin Clayton as the federal postmaster at New Echota.
cases.charges: Residing in the Cherokee Nation without a Georgia license (first Georgia Guard arrest, March 1831).
cases.sentence: Arrested at Carmel, taken through the guard headquarters to Lawrenceville, and discharged the following Saturday because he was then the federal postmaster at New Echota.

name: Elizur Butler
description: Dr. Elizur Butler was a physician and ABCFM missionary in the Cherokee Nation. Convicted with Samuel Worcester on September 15, 1831 for residing there without a Georgia license, he refused the clemency terms and served at hard labor in the Georgia Penitentiary at Milledgeville until his release on January 14, 1833, following the Supreme Court's decision in Worcester v. Georgia. His treatment by the Georgia Guard was notably brutal.

cases.charges: Residing within the Cherokee Nation without a license from the Governor and without taking the oath of allegiance to the State of Georgia, in violation of Georgia's act of December 22, 1830.
cases.sentence: Four years at hard labor. Refused the clemency terms and was committed to the penitentiary at Milledgeville; released January 14, 1833 by Governor Wilson Lumpkin's discharge order following Worcester v. Georgia.

cases.convicted: No — released on bond to appear at the September 1831 court term.
cases.charges: Residing in the Cherokee Nation without a Georgia license (July 1831 arrest by the Georgia Guard).
cases.sentence: Treated with particular severity: a chain was padlocked around his neck and attached to a guard's horse as he was forced to walk after dark; later chained by the ankle to a bedstead and carried to Camp Gilmer. Released on bond July 23, 1831.

name: James J. Trott
description: James J. Trott was a Methodist itinerant missionary in the Cherokee Nation who was arrested at least three times by the Georgia Guard during 1831. Convicted on September 15, 1831 for residing in the Nation without a Georgia license, he was among the nine defendants who accepted clemency and was discharged about September 22, 1831.

cases.charges: Residing within the Cherokee Nation without a license from the Governor and without taking the oath of allegiance to the State of Georgia, in violation of Georgia's act of December 22, 1830.
cases.sentence: Sentenced to four years at hard labor; with eight of the defendants he requested clemency on assurance of not again violating the law and was discharged about September 22, 1831 without being confined inside the penitentiary walls.

cases.charges: Residing in the Cherokee Nation without a Georgia license (July 1831 Georgia Guard arrest).
cases.sentence: Chained by the ankle to another prisoner and repeatedly forced to walk during the transfer to Camp Gilmer; released on bond July 23, 1831.

cases.charges: Residing in the Cherokee Nation without a Georgia license (May 1831 Georgia Guard arrest).
cases.sentence: Marched on a circuitous route of about 110 miles, chained on four successive nights, confined at Camp Gilmer and taken to Lawrenceville; released on bond June 9, 1831.

name: Samuel Mays
description: Samuel Mays (also spelled Mayes) was a white resident of the Cherokee Nation convicted on September 15, 1831 under Georgia's law forbidding white persons to live in Cherokee territory without a state license. Sentenced to four years at hard labor, he accepted clemency and was discharged about September 22, 1831.

cases.charges: Residing within the Cherokee Nation without a license from the Governor and without taking the oath of allegiance to the State of Georgia, in violation of Georgia's act of December 22, 1830.
cases.sentence: Sentenced to four years at hard labor; requested clemency on assurance of not again violating Georgia's law and was discharged about September 22, 1831 without being placed inside the penitentiary walls.

name: John Thompson
description: The Reverend John Thompson was an American Board (ABCFM) missionary in the Cherokee Nation. He was arrested twice by the Georgia Guard during 1831 but was not among the eleven men ultimately sentenced in September.

cases.convicted: No — discharged with Samuel Worcester by Judge Clayton.
cases.charges: Residing in the Cherokee Nation without a Georgia license (March 1831 Georgia Guard arrest).
cases.sentence: Arrested about March 14, 1831 and discharged March 19 with Samuel Worcester when Judge Clayton treated the missionaries as federally authorized agents.

cases.convicted: No — discharged by Colonel John W. A. Sanford minutes after arrival.
cases.charges: Residing in the Cherokee Nation without a Georgia license (June 1831 Georgia Guard arrest).
cases.sentence: Marched some forty to fifty miles, chained by the ankle overnight and briefly placed in the Camp Gilmer jail; Colonel John W. A. Sanford called him out and discharged him within minutes.

name: William McLeod
description: The Reverend William McLeod was superintendent of the Methodist mission in the Cherokee Nation. He had accompanied the July 1831 prisoners to offer assistance and was arrested by the Georgia Guard after criticizing its conduct; he was not among those sentenced in September.

cases.convicted: No — dismissed by Colonel Charles Nelson on July 13, 1831.
cases.charges: Arrested by the Georgia Guard after criticizing its conduct while assisting the July 1831 prisoners.
cases.sentence: Forced to march despite severe pain in his hips, knees and feet; eventually permitted to ride when nearly unable to walk. Colonel Charles Nelson dismissed him July 13 without allowing him to return to say goodbye to the other prisoners.
